pinboard.title: Andrej Karpathy on X: "Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B peo
pinboard.description:
- 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.

- 1-2B (~20%) are casual users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. Many professionals outside of coding are in this tier. This group treats LLMs like a better Google search or a writing aid. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight.

- 20M people (0.2%): professional users of frontier-grade LLMs. 
Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries. 

- ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) have access to frontier-grade systems internally. 
It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind here. 

Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential.

pinboard.title: Can you use autoregressive diffusion to generate market data? (Jane Street)
pinboard.description:
The following is part of a series of posts about 2026 summer intern projects – for more, see “What the interns have wrought, special jumbo 2026 edition”

In quantitative finance we are used to models that take a stream of market data events for a given symbol (like resting orders being added to an order book, cancellations of those orders, executions) and predict that symbol’s future price. Generative models are less common. Imagine a model that could give not just a point estimate of a symbol’s price, but could actually synthesize book events—including the timing of their arrival on the exchange. You’d get price predictions, of course, but your rollouts would have hugely more texture than just that.

But what kind of data is market data? A generative model demands an answer to that question. Is it more like video, or text? That is, is it continuous or discrete? Market data seems to have features of both. An order book evolves via a series of turns as market participants put on, or take away, resting orders; there is no doubt a discrete action space. And yet, many of the most important parameters of a given order, like its price, have such a high cardinality that they basically appear continuous. Some simply are continuous: an easy one to overlook, but crucial for a generative model, is timing, as in “when does the new order arrive at the exchange.” Even that oversimplifies things. In practice the distributions are spiky: “pennying” (where you improve upon a price by one tick) is much more common than improving by two ticks, and orders tend to arrive in bursts, for instance around whole-number times.

One way to explore these complications is to treat your data as if it’s continuous and see how that breaks down. This summer, a research intern, Kavish, built a diffusion model for market data. Diffusion and flow-matching models are powerful tools for representing sequential, multimodal data in regimes such as image, video, robotics, and audio. Taking inspiration from Autoregressive Image Generation without Vector Quantization, Kavish created an event-level generative model of market data using autoregressive diffusion.

There were some technical findings along the way—for example, Kavish found that DDPM, while theoretically ideal for denoising in diffusion models, diverged, and that flow matching performed much better. But the headline result was that fully continuous diffusion did not lend itself to the jaggedness of real market data. Kavish’s various attempts to handle point masses via smoothing, on the one hand, and discretizing some of the model’s targets, on the other, have greatly clarified what an eventual generative model of market data might look like.

pinboard.title: Trump’s Message to Ukraine Is Now Crystal Clear - The Atlantic
pinboard.description:
The president’s actions over the past 72 hours look like an effort to force Kyiv to surrender.
In the past 72 hours, Donald Trump has dropped all pretense, torched a couple decades of American policy, and undermined 18 months of his own diplomacy. He lifted sanctions on the import of Russian diesel fuel, in violation of the letter and spirit of laws that he himself signed. He has threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine, unless Ukraine agrees not to target Russian refineries, thus demanding that Kyiv give up its most effective weapon while asking nothing from Russia in exchange. He has not criticized Russian attacks on Ukrainian power plants or factories, even those owned by American companies. He has offered no condolences for the recent deaths of Ukrainian children in Russian bombing raids.
He has lied repeatedly. He declared that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy cease-fire,” an announcement that surprised the Ukrainians and that in any case the Russians immediately broke, hitting a power plant in Kharkiv only hours later. He accused Ukraine of blocking negotiations, when in reality the Ukrainians have repeatedly proposed cease-fires and Russia has never agreed to a cease-fire or any meaningful negotiation at all.
He has described Ukraine’s democratically elected president as an obstacle to negotiations and told him to leave office. But on Friday, before making these new decisions, he held yet another long, friendly telephone conversation with the Russian dictator, who really could end the war today. All Vladimir Putin has to do is tell his soldiers to stop fighting, and then the war is over. The Ukrainians cannot stop fighting because, if they do, their country will be conquered and they will suffer the fate of their occupied territories: leaders murdered, children kidnapped, repression and concentration camps for everyone else. If Trump knows this, then he does not care.

Ukraine’s drones knock out AI data center belonging to "Russia’s Google" • Ars Technica
pinboard.description:
Jeremy Hsu:

Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to the Russian tech giant Yandex. The damage has left Yandex, known as “Russia’s Google” because it operates the country’s most popular search engine, struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services. The Ukrainian drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions of Russia on October 8 and October 9, according to Reuters. Those actions came as a direct response to a Russian drone strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers, which has disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of Ukrainians since late September. “We continue to respond to Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, and we’re doing so with high precision,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a post on X. “Another data center was hit as well—our symmetrical response.” The Ukrainian company Firepoint said its FP-1 one-way attack drones were involved in the latest strike on the Kaluga data center that is Yandex’s largest such facility, Reuters reported. The first Ukrainian attack targeted Yandex’s Sasovo data center that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers used for training the company’s YandexGPT AI model. Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions to some services. Russian users reported problems accessing media websites and popular apps for the Ivi video streaming platform, the digital banking service T-Bank and the state-owned Russian Railways, according to the independent Russian news publication Meduza. Other impacted Russian services included a dating app, a real estate aggregator, a self-publishing book platform and the website of the most successful professional soccer club in the Russian Premier League, according to Reuters.

It also had the effect of significantly reducing the activity of anonymous politically inflammatory right-wing accounts on various social media platforms. Odd, that. Keep going, Ukraine.
